claim: Evolutionary studies in population genetics and ecology were mainly focused on predicting and understanding past evolutionary events.
source: Evolutionary studies in population genetics and ecology were mainly focused on predicting and understanding past evolutionary events.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical focus of evolutionary studies, presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: A growing trend explores the prediction of evolutionary trajectories toward the future promoted by its wide variety of applications.
source: Recently, however, a growing trend explores the prediction of evolutionary trajectories toward the future promoted by its wide variety of applications.
evidence: This describes a recent trend in the field, based on general knowledge of current research directions.

claim: The present method combines birth-death population models with substitution models that consider selection on protein folding stability.
source: In this context, we introduce a forecasting protein evolution method that integrates birth-death population models with substitution models that consider selection on protein folding stability.
evidence: This is a direct description of the method introduced in the manuscript.

claim: Traditional population genetics methods make the unrealistic assumption of simulating molecular evolution separately from the evolutionary history.
source: In contrast to traditional population genetics methods that usually make the unrealistic assumption of simulating molecular evolution separately from the evolutionary history, the present method combines both processes to simultaneously model forward-in-time birth-death evolutionary trajectories and protein evolution under structurally constrained substitution models that outperformed traditional empirical substitution models.
evidence: This is a characterization of traditional methods and a comparison with the present method, based on knowledge of existing approaches.

claim: Structurally constrained substitution models outperformed traditional empirical substitution models.
source: In contrast to traditional population genetics methods that usually make the unrealistic assumption of simulating molecular evolution separately from the evolutionary history, the present method combines both processes to simultaneously model forward-in-time birth-death evolutionary trajectories and protein evolution under structurally constrained substitution models that outperformed traditional empirical substitution models.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to previous studies and the results presented in this manuscript.

claim: The method showed acceptable errors in predicting the folding stability of the forecasted protein variants.
source: Overall, the method showed acceptable errors in predicting the folding stability of the forecasted protein variants, but, expectedly, the errors were larger in the prediction of the corresponding sequences.
evidence: This is a summary of the results obtained from evaluating the method on viral protein data.

claim: The errors were larger in the prediction of the corresponding sequences compared to folding stability.
source: Overall, the method showed acceptable errors in predicting the folding stability of the forecasted protein variants, but, expectedly, the errors were larger in the prediction of the corresponding sequences.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about prediction errors based on the results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Forecasting protein evolution is feasible in certain evolutionary scenarios.
source: We conclude that forecasting protein evolution is feasible in certain evolutionary scenarios and provide suggestions to enhance its accuracy by improving the underlying models of evolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results of the study.

claim: A variety of biological systems display a Darwinian evolutionary process where selection operates toward a limited set of adapted variants.
source: Nevertheless, a variety of biological systems display a Darwinian evolutionary process where selection operates toward a limited set of adapted variants.
evidence: This is a statement about biological systems based on established evolutionary theory.

claim: Adapted variants and the evolutionary trajectories to reach them would be positively selected and could present a certain degree of predictability.
source: These variants, and in extension the evolutionary trajectories to reach them, would be positively selected and could present a certain degree of predictability (Lässig et al., 2017; Wortel et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Progress in developing more accurate models of evolution motivated investigations on forecasting evolution.
source: The progress made in developing more accurate models of evolution (Arenas, 2015b) and the benefits from predicting the outcome of evolution (i.e. to understand the course of evolution or to prepare for the future Wortel et al., 2023) motivated a variety of investigations on forecasting evolution in diverse fields including medicine, agriculture, biotechnology, and conservation biology, among others (e.g. Barton et al., 2016; Bull and Molineux, 2008; de Visser et al., 2018; Diaz-Uriarte and Vasallo, 2019; Fischer et al., 2015; Gerrish and Sniegowski, 2012; Lässig and Łuksza, 2014; Lind et al., 2019; Luksza and Lässig, 2014; Morris et al., 2018; Munck et al., 2014; Neher et al., 2014; Wortel et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Under neutral evolution, all molecular variants are equally likely to be present in the population, showing lack of repeatability and disallowing accurate prediction of future variants.
source: Under neutral evolution, all the molecular variants are equally likely to be present in the population, showing lack of repeatability and disallowing accurate prediction of future variants.
evidence: This is a statement about neutral evolution based on established evolutionary theory.

claim: Forecasting evolution requires a system with measurable selection pressures.
source: Thus, forecasting evolution requires a system with measurable selection pressures, and where certain positively selected variants could produce more descendants than other variants and expand in the population (Desai and Fisher, 2007; Goyal et al., 2012; Neher and Hallatschek, 2013; Neher et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A rougher fitness landscape resulting from selection can lead to greater accuracy in evolutionary predictions.
source: Actually, a rougher fitness landscape resulting from selection can lead to greater accuracy in evolutionary predictions (Papkou et al., 2023; Rubin et al., 2023; Van Cleve and Weissman, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Protein evolution involves molecular evolutionary processes driven by selection pressures where the fitness of each variant can be parameterized and predicted.
source: Here, we focus on forecasting protein evolution because it involves molecular evolutionary processes driven by selection pressures and where the fitness of each variant can be parameterized and predicted (Carneiro and Hartl, 2010; Gilson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Substitution models that better fit with the study data usually produce more accurate phylogenetic trees and ancestral sequences.
source: The accuracy of these inferences is affected by the accuracy of the applied substitution model, where substitution models that better fit with the study data usually produce more accurate phylogenetic trees and ancestral sequences (Arenas and Bastolla, 2020; Del Amparo and Arenas, 2022a; Lemmon and Moriarty, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SCS models usually demand more computational resources than substitution models that only include information from the protein sequence.
source: In this regard, a variety of studies showed that structurally constrained substitution (SCS) models of protein evolution provide more accurate evolutionary inferences than the traditional empirical substitution models of protein evolution, in terms of phylogenetic likelihood, distribution of amino acid frequencies among protein sites, rates of molecular evolution and folding stability of reconstructed proteins, among other aspects (e.g. Arenas and Bastolla, 2020; Arenas et al., 2016a; Bastolla et al., 2006; Bordner and Mittelmann, 2014; Del Amparo et al., 2023; Echave and Wilke, 2017; Ferreiro et al., 2024a; Ferreiro et al., 2024b; Fornasari et al., 2002; Parisi and Echave, 2001; Pascual-García et al., 2019; Rodrigue et al., 2005), although SCS models usually demand more computational resources than substitution models that only include information from the protein sequence.
evidence: This is a statement about the computational requirements of SCS models based on knowledge of their implementation.

claim: The protein structure provides information about the location and molecular interactions of amino acids at different protein sites.
source: Notice that the protein structure provides information about the location and molecular interactions of amino acids at different protein sites, which could be far from each other in the sequence but close in the three-dimensional structure and interact affecting their evolution (Morcos et al., 2011; Ruiz-González and Fares, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Selection from protein folding stability is relevant in the evolution of multiple proteins, including those in microbial and viral systems.
source: Indeed, selection from the protein folding stability is relevant in the evolution of multiple proteins, including those in microbial and viral systems (e.g. Ferreiro et al., 2022; Gong et al., 2013; Jacquier et al., 2013; Rodrigues et al., 2016; Wylie and Shakhnovich, 2011; Zeldovich et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Traditional population genetics methods apply two separate steps to simulate molecular evolution: first simulating the evolutionary history, then simulating molecular evolution upon that history.
source: In order to simulate molecular evolution, traditional population genetics methods apply two separate steps (Arenas, 2012; Hoban et al., 2012). First, the simulation of the evolutionary history (i.e. a phylogenetic tree) using approaches such as the coalescent and birth-death population processes (Gernhard, 2008; Hudson, 1990; Kingman, 1982; Stadler, 2010). Afterward, the forward-in-time simulation of molecular evolution is performed, from the root node to the tip nodes, upon the previously simulated evolutionary history (Yang, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work describing traditional methods.

claim: Traditional population genetics methods assume that the simulation of the evolutionary history is independent from the simulation of molecular evolution, which can produce biological incoherences.
source: However, for technical and computational simplicity, it assumes that the simulation of the evolutionary history is independent from the simulation of molecular evolution, which can produce biological incoherences (i.e. the evolutionary history is usually simulated under neutral evolution while molecular evolution is usually simulated with substitution models that consider selection).
evidence: This is a critique of traditional methods based on logical inference about their assumptions.

claim: The present method merged evolutionary history simulation and molecular evolution simulation into a single process where evolutionary history influences molecular evolution and vice versa.
source: To enhance the realism of this modeling, here we merged both processes into a single one where evolutionary history influences molecular evolution and vice versa.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach taken in this study.

claim: The method was implemented into a new version of the computer framework ProteinEvolver.
source: The method is detailed below, and we implemented it into a new version of our computer framework ProteinEvolver (Arenas et al., 2013), which is freely available from https://github.com/MiguelArenas/proteinevolver (Arenas, 2025)
evidence: This is a statement about the implementation of the method.

claim: The fitness of a protein variant is calculated from its folding stability following the Boltzmann distribution.
source: The fitness (f) of the protein variant (A) is calculated from its folding stability (free energy, ΔG) following the Boltzmann distribution (Goldstein, 2013) (Equation 1, which takes values from 0 to 1)
evidence: This describes the mathematical approach used in the method, supported by a citation.

claim: Protein folding stability constrains protein evolution and is commonly used to obtain protein fitness.
source: Protein folding stability constrains protein evolution and is commonly used to obtain protein fitness (Bastolla et al., 2007; Goldstein, 2013; Liberles et al., 2012; Lobkovsky et al., 2010; Mendez et al., 2010; Sella and Hirsh, 2005; Zeldovich et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: In nature, high folding stability does not necessarily indicate high fitness, but a stability that closely resembles that of a real protein may suggest high fitness.
source: We believe the latter can be more realistic, as in nature, high folding stability does not necessarily indicate high fitness, but a stability that closely resembles that of a real protein may suggest high fitness since the real stability is the result of a selection process (which also incorporates negative design).
evidence: This is a reasoning about fitness based on biological knowledge and inference.

claim: If the fitness is derived from only the folding stability of the protein variant, the birth rate is considered equal to the fitness.
source: If the fitness is derived from only the folding stability of the protein variant, the birth rate (b) is considered equal to the fitness.
evidence: This describes a specific parameterization in the method.

claim: If the fitness is determined based on the similarity in folding stability between the modeled variant and a real variant, the birth rate is assumed to be 1 minus the RMSD in folding stability.
source: Alternatively, if the fitness is determined based on the similarity in folding stability between the modeled variant and a real variant, the birth rate is assumed to be 1 minus the root mean square deviation (RMSD, which offers advantages such as minimizing the influence of small deviations while amplifying larger differences, thereby enhancing the detection of remarkable molecular changes) in folding stability.
evidence: This describes an alternative parameterization in the method.

claim: In both cases, the death rate is considered as 1-b to allow a constant global (birth-death) rate.
source: In both cases, the death rate (d) is considered as 1-b to allow a constant global (birth-death) rate.
evidence: This describes the parameterization of the death rate in the method.

claim: In the model, the fitness influences reproductive success, where protein variants with higher fitness have higher birth rates leading to more birth events, while those with lower fitness have higher death rates leading to more extinction events.
source: In this model, the fitness influences reproductive success, where protein variants with higher fitness have higher birth rates leading to more birth events, while those with lower fitness have higher death rates leading to more extinction events.
evidence: This describes how fitness affects the birth-death process in the model.

claim: A variant with high fitness does not necessarily accumulate substitutions more rapidly.
source: Although a higher growth rate can sometimes correlate with higher fitness, a variant with high fitness does not necessarily accumulate substitutions more rapidly.
evidence: This is a clarification about the relationship between fitness and substitution rate based on biological reasoning.

claim: Another birth-death model was incorporated that follows the proposal by Neher et al., 2014, in which the death rate is fixed at 1 and the birth rate is modeled as 1+fitness.
source: Additionally, we incorporated another birth-death model that follows the proposal by Neher et al., 2014, in which the death rate is fixed at 1 and the birth rate is modeled as 1+fitness.
evidence: This describes an alternative model implementation based on a cited work.

claim: In the variable-rate model, fitness not only affects reproductive success but also influences the global birth-death rate, which can vary among lineages.
source: In this model, fitness not only affects reproductive success but also influences the global birth-death rate, which can vary among lineages.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the variable-rate birth-death model.

claim: In contrast to standard birth-death processes where birth and death rates are constant over time and among lineages, the present method considers heterogeneity where each protein variant at a node has specific birth and death rates according to its corresponding fitness.
source: In contrast to standard birth-death processes where birth and death rates are constant over time and among lineages, the present method considers heterogeneity where each protein variant at a node has specific birth and death rates according to its corresponding fitness.
evidence: This describes a key difference between the present method and standard birth-death processes.

claim: The process simultaneously simulates, forward in time, evolutionary history and protein evolution, with protein evolution influencing the evolutionary history through selection from the folding stability.
source: This process simultaneously simulates, forward in time, evolutionary history and protein evolution, with protein evolution influencing the evolutionary history through selection from the folding stability.
evidence: This describes the integrated nature of the simulation process.
